props.title: As Tears Go By
props.initialSlug: Gangster torn between love and loyalty in Hong Kong

sections.content: Wong Kar-wai's electrifying directorial debut **As Tears Go By** (1988) revolutionized Hong Kong cinema by infusing triad crime drama with art house sensibilities. Taking cues from Martin Scorsese's **Mean Streets** (1973), Wong transforms the neon-drenched streets of Hong Kong into a moody canvas for exploring loyalty, doomed romance, and urban alienation. Andy Lau's portrayal of Wah, a mid-level gangster torn between duty to his volatile "brother" Fly and his growing love for his cousin Ngor, established a template for the conflicted antiheroes that would populate Wong's later masterpieces like **Chungking Express** (1994) and **Fallen Angels** (1995).

sections.content: The film's visual style marks the beginning of Wong's distinctive aesthetic approach, though not yet fully formed. Cinematographer Andrew Lau (who would later direct **Infernal Affairs** [2002]) brings a kinetic energy to the action sequences while finding poetry in quiet moments. The use of step-printing - a technique of shooting at a lower frame rate then printing at normal speed - creates dreamlike sequences that would become Wong's signature. This technical innovation perfectly captures the psychological state of characters living on society's edges.

While **As Tears Go By** adheres more closely to genre conventions than Wong's later work, it contains the seeds of themes he would explore throughout his career. Like **Days of Being Wild** (1990) and **In the Mood for Love** (2000), the film examines how time and fate conspire against romance. Maggie Cheung's performance as Ngor brings vulnerability and depth to what could have been a standard "girlfriend role," beginning her transformation into one of world cinema's most compelling actresses. SUBHEAD: The Birth of Urban Melancholy Cinema

sections.content: Wong's treatment of Hong Kong itself proved hugely influential on subsequent Asian cinema. The city becomes a character, its cramped apartments and neon-lit streets reflecting the emotional claustrophobia of its inhabitants. This approach influenced a generation of filmmakers, from Taiwanese director Hou Hsiao-hsien's **Millennium Mambo** (2001) to Korean auteur Park Chan-wook's **Oldboy** (2003). The film's mix of commercial appeal and artistic ambition created a template for Hong Kong's Second Wave cinema movement.
